query: For a high-entropy alloy designed as a single-phase solid solution and exhibiting a favorable strength–ductility combination, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading? Explain the hypothesized mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the same alloy tested under identical conditions without the intervention, define the applicable exposure and loading regime, identify supporting evidence from prior observations, and specify an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a second phase assisted by the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect can preserve toughness in a high-entropy alloy after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
generation.intervention: Introduction of a second phase assisted by the TRIP effect
generation.baseline: Same alloy without the introduction of a second phase
generation.uncertainty: The exact conditions and mechanisms by which the TRIP effect preserves toughness are not fully understood and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the toughness of a high-entropy alloy with and without the introduction of a second phase after thermal exposure and subsequent loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the alloy with the introduced second phase is not significantly higher than that of the alloy without the second phase, the hypothesis is falsified

Own digest: Exceptional damage-tolerance of a medium-entropy alloy CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are an intriguing new class of metallic materials that derive their properties from being multi-element systems that can crystallize as a single phase, despite containing high concentrations of five or more elements with different crystal structures. Here we examine an equiatomic medium-entropy alloy containing only three elements, CrCoNi, as a single-phase face-centred cubic solid solution, which displays strength-toughness properties that exceed those of all high-entropy alloys and most multi-phase alloys. At room temperature, the alloy shows tensile strengths of almost 1 GPa, failure strains of ∼70% and KJIc fracture-toughness values above 200 MPa m1/2; at cryogenic temperatures strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength level
